new_statements.rule_in_words: According to Bennett's survey, Hofling's 2011 dictionary describes Mopan word stress as falling on the initial syllable of the root (i.e. anchored to the lexical root rather than to the word edge, so prefixed material is unstressed). Bennett gives no examples or further detail for Mopan; the sentence closes a paragraph on languages whose fixed stress is shifted by phrase position, but no such phrasal shift is actually attributed to Mopan.
new_statements.exceptions: None mentioned. Footnote 21 attached to the sentence only notes Fox (1978) arguing that proto-Mayan had initial stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level ('root-initial'); nothing on citation forms vs. phrases. Second-hand: the primary statement is in Hofling 2011 (User's Guide pp. 3-32), which could not be opened.
new_statements.identity_note: mopa1243 is language-level with no Glottolog dialect subdivisions. Hofling's 2011 data (the source behind the statement) come from fieldwork in San Luis, Petén, Guatemala (Hofling 2007: 1); Sobrino Gómez 2021 is also Guatemalan Mopan. Belizean Mopan (Toledo District) is not separately described in any source seen. Glottolog's listing of Zavala 1974 'Gramatica maya' (Mérida) under mopa1243 looks like a Yucatec item and was not pursued.

new_statements.quote: In all of the languages, the stress falls on the final syllable of the word. When a combination of words is spoken, the stronger stress falls at the end of the utterance, though there is still a noticeable stress at the end of each word. As the utterance proceeds, the intensity of the sentence increases and the final stress is the dominant one in the stream of speech. This stress placement, the rise and fall of levels of intonation, and the sharpness of the glottal stop common to these languages combine to produce a characteristic speech pattern markedly different from the syllable-timed rhythm of Spanish.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog's existing statement (Bennett 2016 reporting Hofling 2011: root-initial stress; Hofling 2011 User's Guide 1.2.4.1: 'Lexical stress falls on the first syllable of the root and on alternate syllables. Syllables with long vowels (CVVC) or glottalized vowels (CV'[V]C) are always stressed') places stress at the start of the root. Mayers's 1966 introduction says stress is word-final in 'all of the languages' of the volume, Mopan among them. The two differ in placement (final vs root-initial) and in type (fixed vs morphologically anchored). Weight is low: it is an editorial generalization, not a finding of the Mopan chapter, and the Ulrich & Ulrich chapter is silent. Caveat on 'silent'…
new_statements.rule_in_words: The only stress statement in the volume that covers Mopan is the editor's blanket claim in the Introduction: in all of the languages described (Mopan included, ch. XI) word stress falls on the final syllable of the word; in connected speech the strongest stress goes to the end of the utterance while each word keeps a weaker final stress. The Mopan chapter itself (Ulrich & Ulrich, pp. 251-271) yielded no statement on stress, accent, tone, pitch or juncture; its phoneme footnote (p. 261) lists long vowels a·, u· etc. but no stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: No word-level secondary stress described. Phrase level only: 'the stronger stress falls at the end of the utterance, though there is still a noticeable stress at the end of each word' (p. 14).
new_statements.exceptions: None stated; the claim is a blanket generalization over all fourteen languages in the volume. The volume's only language-specific stress descriptions are in ch. VII Mam (Sywulka): CVCV verb stems with first-syllable stress vs CVC.CV- stems with second-syllable stress, reduplicated CVCCVC stems stressed on the second syllable, and the passive -t/-it/-et and infinitive -b'il/-l/-el/-il allomorphs conditioned by stress position; these are Mam, not Mopan.
new_statements.identity_note: The Ulrich & Ulrich chapter describes the Mopan Maya of Guatemala (Petén; the intro's census list gives 'Mopan 2,500'; the ethnography mentions Mopan Maya-Kekchi and Mopan Maya-Ladino mixed populations). No dialect is named in the fragments seen. The editor's stress statement is about 'all of the languages' in the volume, not a Mopan variety specifically. The five stem-class stress passages first surfaced by the Mopan-anchored searches were verified (examples b'incha- 'to make', elk'a- 'to steal', tu'n, ma c'met, -njts, yoli- 'to speak', -b'il) to belong to ch. VII Mam (pp. 166-195), not to ch. XI Mopan.

readall_conflicts: One disagreement. Mayers's editorial Introduction to Languages of Guatemala (1966, p. 14) states that in all of the languages covered, Mopan included, stress falls on the final syllable of the word, with the strongest stress at the end of the utterance. The catalog's existing statement (Bennett 2016, citing Hofling 2011) and Hofling 2011's own User's Guide give root-initial stress with alternate-syllable stress and obligatory stress on long- or glottalized-vowel syllables. The Ulrich & Ulrich Mopan chapter itself, as far as the full-text index exposes it, says nothing about stress, so the 1966 claim for Mopan rests only on the editor's blanket generalization, which is typical of the K'ichean, Mamean and Q'anjob'alan languages that dominate the volume; it should not displace Hofling's Mopan-specific description. All language-specific stress passages found in the volume belong to the Mam grammar (Sywulka) and describe Mam stem classes, not Mopan.
